extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, historians of geometry, and mathematicians interested in diagrammatic reasoning and foundations
extracted.subtask_description: Reconstructing and articulating standards for producing and reading diagrams in Euclidean (plane) geometry so as to justify diagram-based inferences and assess their role in rigorous proofs. Focuses on inferential roles, production standards, and how diagram and discursive text share responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagrams license inference
rubrics_metrics.description: In Euclidean geometry, a diagram has standing to license inference, just as do relationships recognized in the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat diagrams as genuinely inferential 'textual' elements: they contribute to the justificatory structure of proofs and so require explicit standards for how diagram-based inferences are licensed and used in the discursive argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of responsibility between diagram and text
rubrics_metrics.description: A practice must divide responsibility so that the discursive text records and resolves features (e.g., equalities) that cannot be uniformly read off from imperfect physical diagrams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the text to track equality information and other exact relations that physical diagram production cannot uniformly guarantee; this division is a way to attain uniformity of response despite variation in physical diagrams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attain uniformity of response
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants are responsible for attaining uniformity of response in reading off features in diagrams, even though production/reading cannot be directly controlled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practice must provide means (procedures, textual attributions, conventions) to resolve differences in participants' responses to reasonably producible diagrams, since direct human control over diagrams is limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repertoire restriction (limited basic responsive roles)
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful geometric practice limits the repertoire of basic responsive roles it requires (e.g., recognizing a triangle and ~30 other items).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restricting the set of required recognitions makes stable shared responses feasible; this repertoire is drastically less diverse than the full space of physical or imagined diagrams and supports reliable cooperative reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generality via uniform artifact strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Generality is achieved either by restricting the diversity of artifact responses or by producing more uniform artifacts so that one diagram covers many instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Later geometries (Descartes, projective) exploit such uniformity to reduce case-branching; achieve uniformity either by reducing diversity of artifacts or responses, but be cautious—over-uniformization can eliminate distinctions necessary for correct reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unsuitable limitation that blinds practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Unsuitable limitation of the artifact-and-response repertoire leaves a practice blind and irrelevant by failing to support distinctions where different actions are required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not collapse distinctions that could be relevant in future stages of a proof; Euclidean diagrams 'write p1' until a possible p' would require a different response, forcing case distinctions and possibly multiple diagrams.

rubrics_metrics.name: One proof, one geometric reasoning context (preferred)
rubrics_metrics.description: Euclidean argument tends to prefer 'one proof, one genuinely geometric reasoning context'—roughly 'one proof, one diagram'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Except for logical unpacking that would require nested contexts, prefer a single reasoning context per demonstration in which a diagram plays a special role. Disjunctive case-analysis may require distinct diagrams, but this is not the preferred route.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagrams are not straightforward semantic counterparts in reductio contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs by contradiction (reductio) never admit a semantics in which each claim in force in the reductio context is jointly true, so a semantic relation treating a diagram as a perfect counterpart is incompatible with reductio use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ontological/semantic strategies that treat diagrams as literal, jointly-compatible representations of all claims in a reductio context; instead, address the problem via inferential standards for diagram use (diagram semantics cannot simply solve reductio issues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagram-based attribution criteria (three-part test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Features may be directly attributable from the diagram only if they (a) have explicit perceptual cues, (b) are fairly stable across a range of variation of diagram (co-exact rather than exact), and (c) are not readily eliminable by diagram discipline (skillful drawing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this three-part test to decide which diagram features license direct attributions in the text. If a feature lacks these properties, it should not be taken as diagram-licensed without further textual support or construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appearance/topology determines attributable features
rubrics_metrics.description: The appearance or topology of a diagram—its inclusions and contiguities of regions, segments, and points (insofar as not eliminable by diagram discipline)—determines which features are attributable from the diagram.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat region inclusion and contiguity relations as primary for attribution; these topological aspects are the stable core from which readable diagram-based inferences arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagram discipline: some features eliminable, some not
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain features of a diagram can be eliminated or altered by better diagram-discipline (skill in drawing), while others are robust against such discipline and hence attributable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reconstructing standards, distinguish features susceptible to drawing-improvement (not trustworthy as direct attributions) from robust features that persist across disciplined diagram production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagrams provide existential import with continuity and exact relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuity considerations enforced by the diagram, together with exact relations, often supply existential content (e.g., constructing a diagonal in a rectangle yields new triangles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge that diagrams can contribute existential conclusions not readily obtained from discursive text alone; modern formalisms (Hilbert, Tarski) capture some of this by strengthening text, but traditional practice relied on diagrammatic continuity plus exact relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of regions in Greek diagram interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Greek geometry treats diagrams as made up primarily of regions (figures as contained by boundaries) rather than primarily as delimiting curves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reconstructing ancient Euclidean practice, attend to region-based interpretation: the relevant perceptual/attributable features are about contained regions and their relations, not merely the bounding curves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Augment discursive text with explicit diagram-production and -reading standards
rubrics_metrics.description: To account for diagram-based inference, one must augment the logical construal of the discursive text by reconstructing explicit standards for producing and reading diagrams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical texts give little explicit discussion; reconstructive work should draw on recorded disputes, case objections, and the interplay between diagram and text to make these standards explicit and usable in justificatory accounts.
